title: LLM Training Pipeline End-to-End
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# LLM Training Pipeline End-to-End ##### The loss spike at step 14,200 A team in Bengaluru was 61 hours into a pretraining run on 8×A100 — roughly ₹1.9 lakh of GPU time — when the loss went from 2.84 to 9.1 in four steps, then flattened at 10.4 and never recovered. They restarted from the last checkpoint. Same thing at the same step. That reproducibility was the clue. A random hardware fault would not recur at the identical step; a **data problem** would. They pulled the batch at step 14,200 and found a single document of 40,000 repeated `\x00` bytes — a corrupted file that had survived their ingestion filters. Every token in that sequence was the same, the model's loss on it was enormous, and the resulting gradient blew the weights out of their trained basin. The fix took two lines: a length-normalised entropy filter in the data pipeline, and `max_grad_norm=1.0` in the trainer. **The gradient clipping alone would have saved the run.** They had left it out because the config they copied did not have it. Training LLMs is not conceptually hard — Day 14 covered the optimisation. It is *operationally* hard, and the operational knowledge is what separates a run that finishes from ₹1.9 lakh of wasted GPU time. That is today. ##### The pipeline ```mermaid flowchart TD A["Raw corpus"] --> B["Filter: length, entropy,
dedup, quality"] B --> C["Tokenize + pack
into fixed blocks"] C --> D["Shard to disk
memory-mapped"] D --> E["DataLoader
shuffle, prefetch"] E --> F["Training step:
fwd → loss → bwd → clip → opt"] F --> G["LR scheduler step"] G --> H{"Every N steps"} H -->|log| I["W&B: loss, LR, grad_norm,
MFU, tokens/sec"] H -->|eval| J["Held-out loss"] H -->|save| K["Checkpoint:
model + optim + scheduler + RNG"] K --> F I --> L{"Loss spike?"} L -->|yes| M["Inspect the batch,
rewind to checkpoint,
skip data"] ``` ##### Data loading and packing Naive batching pads every sequence to the batch maximum. With variable-length documents that wastes an enormous fraction of your compute on padding tokens. **Packing** concatenates documents with an EOS separator and slices into fixed-length blocks. Zero padding, 100% token utilisation. ```python import numpy as np from pathlib import Path def pack_and_shard(texts, tokenizer, block_size=2048, shard_tokens=100_000_000, out_dir="data/shards"): """Tokenize, concatenate with EOS, write uint16 shards to disk.""" Path(out_dir).mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) eos = tokenizer.eos_token_id buffer, shard_idx, written = [], 0, 0 for text in texts: ids = tokenizer.encode(text, add_special_tokens=False) buffer.extend(ids + [eos]) while len(buffer) >= shard_tokens: arr = np.array(buffer[:shard_tokens], dtype=np.uint16) arr.tofile(f"{out_dir}/shard_{shard_idx:05d}.bin") buffer = buffer[shard_tokens:] shard_idx += 1 written += shard_tokens if buffer: np.array(buffer, dtype=np.uint16).tofile(f"{out_dir}/shard_{shard_idx:05d}.bin") return written ``` **`uint16` requires a vocabulary under 65,536** — true for most models, and it halves your disk footprint versus `uint32`. Check before you commit to it. ```python import torch from torch.utils.data import Dataset class PackedDataset(Dataset): """Memory-mapped so a 500GB corpus needs no RAM.""" def __init__(self, shard_paths, block_size=2048): self.block_size = block_size self.shards = [np.memmap(p, dtype=np.uint16, mode="r") for p in shard_paths] self.lengths = [len(s) // block_size for s in self.shards] self.cumulative = np.cumsum([0] + self.lengths) def __len__(self): return int(self.cumulative[-1]) def __getitem__(self, idx): shard_i = int(np.searchsorted(self.cumulative, idx, side="right") - 1) local = idx - self.cumulative[shard_i] start = local * self.block_size chunk = self.shards[shard_i][start : start + self.block_size + 1] x = torch.from_numpy(chunk[:-1].astype(np.int64)) y = torch.from_numpy(chunk[1:].astype(np.int64)) # ← the shift return x, y ``` **The `[:-1]` / `[1:]` shift is next-token prediction.** Get it wrong and the model learns the identity function — loss drops implausibly fast in the first hundred steps, which is your signal to check. **One caveat with packing:** documents bleed across block boundaries, so the model occasionally attends across an unrelated document boundary. Most pretraining accepts this; for SFT it matters more, and you should either use document-boundary attention masking or accept short padded sequences. **Data quality filters** are what would have prevented the Bengaluru spike: ```python import math from collections import Counter def quality_filter(text: str, min_len=200, max_len=200_000, min_entropy=2.5, max_repeat_ratio=0.25) -> bool: if not (min_len <= len(text) <= max_len): return False counts = Counter(text) n = len(text) entropy = -sum((c / n) * math.log2(c / n) for c in counts.values()) if entropy < min_entropy: # catches the \x00 document return False lines = text.split("\n") if lines and len(set(lines)) / len(lines) < (1 - max_repeat_ratio): return False return True ``` Add near-duplicate removal (MinHash/LSH) and PII scrubbing. Deduplication in particular is worth real effort — Lee et al. showed it improves quality *and* reduces memorisation of training data. ##### Learning rate schedules The learning rate is the single most consequential hyperparameter, and its *schedule* matters as much as its peak value. ```python import math def lr_at_step(step, max_lr=3e-4, min_lr=3e-5, warmup_steps=2000, total_steps=100_000): """Linear warmup then cosine decay — the standard schedule.""" if step < warmup_steps: return max_lr * (step + 1) / warmup_steps if step > total_steps: return min_lr progress = (step - warmup_steps) / (total_steps - warmup_steps) coeff = 0.5 * (1.0 + math.cos(math.pi * progress)) return min_lr + coeff * (max_lr - min_lr) ``` **Warmup is not optional.** At initialisation, Adam's second-moment estimate `v` is near zero, so the effective step size `m/√v` is enormous and erratic. A full-size step in the first hundred iterations can permanently damage the weights. Use 1–2% of total steps, or roughly 2,000 steps. **Cosine decay to about 10% of peak** is the convention. Decaying to exactly zero slightly hurts; a floor helps the model keep making small refinements. **Choosing the peak LR.** A workable heuristic from the scaling-law literature: $$\text{lr}_{\text{peak}} \approx 0.003 \cdot \left(\frac{d_{\text{model}}}{1024}\right)^{-0.5}$$ Larger models want smaller learning rates. Typical values: 6e-4 for a 124M model, 3e-4 at 1B, 1.5e-4 at 7B, 1e-4 at 70B. **Batch size and LR scale together.** McCandlish et al.'s critical-batch-size work formalises this; the practical rule is that doubling batch size supports roughly `√2` to `2×` the learning rate. Beyond the critical batch size, larger batches stop improving convergence per token and you are just burning compute. ##### Gradient accumulation and clipping You want a large effective batch — typically 0.5M to 4M tokens for pretraining — and your GPU holds far less. ```python accum_steps = target_tokens_per_batch // (micro_batch * block_size * world_size) model.train() optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True) for step in range(total_steps): for micro in range(accum_steps): x, y = next(loader) x, y = x.to(device, non_blocking=True), y.to(device, non_blocking=True) # Only sync gradients across DDP ranks on the LAST microstep if hasattr(model, "no_sync") and micro < accum_steps - 1: ctx = model.no_sync() else: ctx = contextlib.nullcontext() with ctx, torch.autocast(device_type="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16): logits = model(x) loss = F.cross_entropy(logits.view(-1, logits.size(-1)), y.view(-1)) loss = loss / accum_steps # ← average, don't sum loss.backward() grad_norm = torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), max_norm=1.0) lr = lr_at_step(step) for g in optimizer.param_groups: g["lr"] = lr optimizer.step() optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True) ``` **Three details that matter:** - **`loss / accum_steps`** — without it, your effective gradient is `accum_steps` times too large. - **`no_sync()`** on all but the last microstep avoids an all-reduce per microstep, which is a substantial speedup in distributed training. - **`clip_grad_norm_` returns the pre-clip norm.** Log it. **This is the single most valuable training diagnostic**, and it is the metric that would have shown the Bengaluru team a warning several steps before their loss exploded. **Use bf16, not fp16, on Ampere or newer.** bf16 has the same exponent range as fp32, so it does not need loss scaling and does not silently overflow. fp16 requires a `GradScaler` and is a source of subtle instability. ##### Checkpointing A checkpoint that saves only model weights is not resumable. ```python def save_checkpoint(path, model, optimizer, scheduler, step, tokens_seen, config): torch.save({ "step": step, "tokens_seen": tokens_seen, "model": model.state_dict(), "optimizer": optimizer.state_dict(), # Adam m and v — essential "scheduler": scheduler.state_dict() if scheduler else None, "config": config, "rng_python": random.getstate(), "rng_numpy": np.random.get_state(), "rng_torch": torch.get_rng_state(), "rng_cuda": torch.cuda.get_rng_state_all(), }, path) def load_checkpoint(path, model, optimizer, scheduler, map_location="cuda"): ckpt = torch.load(path, map_location=map_location) model.load_state_dict(ckpt["model"]) optimizer.load_state_dict(ckpt["optimizer"]) if scheduler and ckpt["scheduler"]: scheduler.load_state_dict(ckpt["scheduler"]) random.setstate(ckpt["rng_python"]) np.random.set_state(ckpt["rng_numpy"]) torch.set_rng_state(ckpt["rng_torch"]) torch.cuda.set_rng_state_all(ckpt["rng_cuda"]) return ckpt["step"], ckpt["tokens_seen"] ``` **Omitting the optimizer state causes a visible loss spike on resume**, because Adam's momentum buffers restart from zero. It looks like a bug in your model; it is a bug in your checkpointing. **Also save the dataloader position.** Otherwise resuming replays data the model has already seen, which biases training subtly. Practical cadence: checkpoint every 30–60 minutes, keep the last three plus every tenth, and write asynchronously to object storage so you do not stall the training loop. ##### Loss spikes and divergence ```mermaid flowchart TD A["Loss spike observed"] --> B{"grad_norm spiked
in preceding steps?"} B -->|Yes, gradually| C["LR too high →
lower peak, longer warmup"] B -->|Yes, suddenly| D["Bad data batch →
inspect it"] B -->|No| E{"Reproducible at
the same step?"} E -->|Yes| D E -->|No| F["Hardware / numerical →
check for NaN, try bf16"] D --> G["Filter the data,
rewind, skip those steps"] C --> H["Rewind to checkpoint,
reduce LR, resume"] ``` **Detection and automatic response:** ```python class SpikeGuard: def __init__(self, window=100, loss_factor=2.0, gnorm_factor=5.0): self.losses, self.gnorms = [], [] self.window = window self.loss_factor, self.gnorm_factor = loss_factor, gnorm_factor def check(self, loss, grad_norm, step): alerts = [] if len(self.losses) >= self.window: median_loss = statistics.median(self.losses[-self.window:]) median_gn = statistics.median(self.gnorms[-self.window:]) if loss > median_loss * self.loss_factor: alerts.append(f"loss spike: {loss:.3f} vs median {median_loss:.3f}") if grad_norm > median_gn * self.gnorm_factor: alerts.append(f"grad_norm spike: {grad_norm:.1f} vs {median_gn:.1f}") if math.isnan(loss) or math.isinf(loss): alerts.append("NaN/Inf loss") self.losses.append(loss) self.gnorms.append(grad_norm) return alerts ``` **The recovery playbook, in order:** 1. **Rewind** to the last good checkpoint — usually 100–500 steps back. 2. **Skip the offending data.** If the spike reproduces at the same step, it is the batch. 3. **Lower the LR** by 2–5× and re-warm over a few hundred steps. 4. **Tighten clipping** to 0.5. 5. **Check for numerical issues** — bf16 rather than fp16, and confirm no `inf` in the attention scores. **Preventative measures that cost nothing:** always clip gradients, always warm up, use bf16, apply z-loss regularisation on the output logits (`1e-4 · log²(Z)`) to keep them from drifting large, and filter your data properly. ##### Weights & Biases logging ```python import wandb wandb.init( project="gpt-pretrain", name=f"gpt-124m-{run_id}", config={ "d_model": 768, "n_layers": 12, "n_heads": 12, "block_size": 1024, "vocab_size": 50304, "max_lr": 6e-4, "min_lr": 6e-5, "warmup_steps": 2000, "batch_tokens": 524_288, "total_steps": 100_000, "weight_decay": 0.1, "grad_clip": 1.0, "dtype": "bfloat16", }, ) def log_step(step, loss, grad_norm, lr, tokens_seen, dt, n_params, cfg): tokens_per_sec = cfg["batch_tokens"] / dt flops_per_token = 6 * n_params + 12 * cfg["n_layers"] * cfg["block_size"] * cfg["d_model"] mfu = (flops_per_token * tokens_per_sec) / (312e12 * torch.cuda.device_count()) wandb.log({ "train/loss": loss, "train/perplexity": math.exp(min(loss, 20)), "train/grad_norm": grad_norm, # ← watch this one "train/lr": lr, "perf/tokens_per_sec": tokens_per_sec, "perf/mfu": mfu, "perf/step_time_ms": dt * 1000, "progress/tokens_seen": tokens_seen, }, step=step) ``` **The five metrics to actually watch:** | Metric | Healthy | Warning sign | |---|---|---| | `train/loss` | Smooth decrease | Sudden jump, or flat | | `train/grad_norm` | Stable, 0.1–2.0 | Rising trend or spikes | | `perf/mfu` | 0.35–0.55 | Below 0.2 = a bottleneck | | `val/loss` | Tracks train | Diverging = overfitting | | `perf/tokens_per_sec` | Constant | Dropping = data loader stall | **`grad_norm` is the leading indicator.** It typically rises for several steps before the loss visibly spikes, which is your window to intervene. **MFU below 0.2** almost always means the data loader is starving the GPU. Check `num_workers`, `pin_memory=True`, and `prefetch_factor` before assuming you need better kernels. ##### Common mistakes - **No gradient clipping** — the ₹1.9 lakh lesson. - **No warmup**, diverging in the first hundred steps. - **Forgetting `loss / accum_steps`.** - **Checkpointing without optimizer state**, producing a spike on resume. - **Not saving the dataloader position**, replaying seen data. - **fp16 instead of bf16** on modern hardware. - **No data quality filtering.** - **Not logging `grad_norm`**, losing your best early-warning signal. - **Missing the target shift**, learning the identity function. - **Padding instead of packing**, wasting a large fraction of compute. - **LR scaled for a small model** applied to a large one. - **No held-out validation set**, so you cannot distinguish memorisation from learning. - **Ignoring MFU** and buying more GPUs to fix a data loader problem. ##### Hands-on: launch and instrument Your practical task configures and launches a small pretraining run with warmup, cosine decay, clipping, and W&B logging. Use nanoGPT as the base. Before starting, write down your expected loss at step 1 — it should be approximately `ln(vocab_size)`, about 10.8 for a 50K vocabulary. If your first-step loss is far from that, something is wrong with initialisation or the target shift, and finding it now saves hours. The mini project pretrains a small GPT, deliberately induces a loss spike, and documents the diagnosis. Inject a corrupted document — a few thousand repeated bytes — at a known position in your data. Run once without clipping and watch it destroy the run; run again with `max_grad_norm=1.0` and watch it survive. Screenshot both W&B loss curves side by side. That comparison is the most convincing artefact you can produce on this topic. The assignment is a training runbook covering hyperparameter selection, monitoring, and failure recovery. Write it as an operational document a teammate could follow at 2am: a table of hyperparameters by model size, the five metrics to watch with their thresholds, and a decision tree for spikes, NaN, OOM, and MFU collapse. Include the specific commands to rewind and resume. That runbook is exactly the artefact a hiring manager for an infra role wants to see. ##### Key takeaways - **Always clip gradients and always warm up.** Both are one line, and either one alone would have saved a 61-hour run. - **Pack sequences into fixed blocks with memory-mapped shards** — padding wastes compute, and `uint16` halves your disk. - **Log `grad_norm`, not just loss.** It rises before the loss spikes, giving you a window to intervene. - **Checkpoint the optimizer state, scheduler, RNG, and dataloader position** — anything less produces a mysterious spike on resume. - **A reproducible spike at the same step means bad data**, not bad hardware; filter by entropy and repetition, and inspect the batch before you touch hyperparameters.
